input.question: Why does a hearing a recording of my voice sound different to me then when I hear myself talk?
input.ground_truth: We hear sounds as vibrations hitting our ear drums. When we hear most sounds, these vibrations travel through the air and into the ear canal. Our own voices also vibrate through our bodies, creating a slightly lower pitch. When you hear a recording of your voice you are missing this extra level of vibration that lowers the sound, so your voice sounds higher than what you are used to. Source: _URL_0_

response.prediction: When you speak, your voice reaches your ears in two ways: through vibrations traveling *inside* your head (via your bones and tissues), which makes your voice sound deeper and richer to yourself, and through the air, which is how others hear it. A recording only captures the sound waves traveling through the air, so it sounds higher-pitched and less resonant than what you’re used to hearing internally. This difference is normal and happens to everyone—your brain is just comparing the familiar "inside" version to the unfamiliar "outside" recording!
